clue.text: Dior's the last word in fashion?

definitions.text: Dior's the last word in fashion?

parts.words: Dior's the last word in fashion?
parts.note: surface reading: praise for the couturier as the ultimate in style; setter's reading: a French phrase, fitting for Dior, literally meaning 'last cry' and used for the newest style

explanation.surface: A fan declares the Paris fashion house Dior the height of style.
explanation.walkthrough: Dior is French, so the latest fashion is given in French: DERNIER CRI, literally 'last cry'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French expression is borrowed into English for the very latest style or trend in clothes.

clue.text: Vagrant, extremely destitute old widow

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the next word, its first and last letters

parts.note: relict is an archaic word for a widow

explanation.surface: A homeless person is described as a very poor old widow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for destitute but asks for that word's outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A derelict is a homeless down-and-out person, a noun that means much the same as a vagrant.

clue.text: Jack has drop of Armagnac after port wine

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a port
J is the card abbreviation for jack

indicators.note: a drop is just a tiny amount, so only the opening letter of the brandy's name is taken

explanation.surface: Jack takes a nip of brandy after drinking port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink but is a harbour city; 'after' puts the jack-and-brandy pair after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a red or white Spanish table wine from the region of that name.

clue.text: Also against article on pub acquisition

parts.note: to run into something is to go against it

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a newspaper piece about a brewery buying up a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' means placed above, so the article sits over the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Into the bargain is an idiom for in addition, a phrase meaning the same as also.

clue.text: Strange term involving a particular kind of painter

indicators.note: involving means wrapping up within, so one piece is enclosed by the other
strange means odd or unusual, so the letters come out in an unusual order

parts.note: a brand is a particular kind or make of product

explanation.surface: An art critic uses an odd word for one type of painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A particular kind of painter' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'painter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt was the great seventeenth-century Dutch artist, so his name stands for a painter.

clue.text: Run over English international after start of race

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a cap is a player chosen for their national team

explanation.surface: An England player is knocked down by a car just as a race begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' suggests a road accident; it means go over again briefly. A cap is awarded to a player each time they represent their country.
explanation.definitionFit: To recap is to summarise the main points again, which is to run over them.

clue.text: Unsatisfactory, a bygone king

parts.note: food or a performance that is off is not up to standard

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses an old monarch as a poor ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' does double duty in the surface but belongs to the wordplay; the definition is 'bygone king'. Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, famous for Offa's Dyke.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia in the 700s, so he is a king from long ago.

clue.text: Tell age of specially designed musical instrument

indicators.note: something specially designed has been made up afresh, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An expert is asked to date a custom-made instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A flageolet is a small wind instrument like a recorder, a type of musical instrument.

clue.text: Relaxed with drop of Scotch (last from bottle) following a meal

parts.note: tea is an evening meal in parts of Britain

indicators.note: a drop is only a small amount, so just the opening letter of the spirit is used
the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: After dinner someone unwinds with the dregs of the whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts the two single letters after A and TEA. In Britain tea can mean the main evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: At ease means free from tension or anxiety, an idiom for relaxed.

clue.text: Those offering help with anagrams do it so furtively

indicators.note: done furtively means done in a sly, crooked way, so the letters are bent out of order

explanation.surface: Crossword helpers sneakily solve the anagrams for you.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue cheekily uses the word 'anagrams' as its own fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Good Samaritans are people who help strangers in need, from Jesus's parable, so they are helpers.

clue.text: Temporary place to stay, very large, in decay

indicators.note: the decay word holds the size abbreviation within it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: A traveller finds a huge but crumbling building to stay in for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is where a bird settles for the night, and by extension any temporary lodging.

clue.text: One bird and a piece of veal taken in by me from oven

indicators.note: being taken in means being received inside, so the whole run goes within the outer word

parts.note: taken as written; it is the outer word

indicators.note: a piece is only a small bit, so just the opening letter of the meat is taken

explanation.surface: A cook takes a bird and some veal out of the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything from 'One' to 'veal' goes inside ME. 'From' here only joins wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A microwave is a kitchen appliance that heats food, a kind of oven.

clue.text: Jumped in field — prelude to training?

parts.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
PT, physical training, is the warm-up exercise that precedes real training; the question mark flags the loose sense

explanation.surface: An athlete bounds across a field as a warm-up before practice.
explanation.walkthrough: PT stands for physical training, school gym or army exercise; the setter playfully casts it as the curtain-raiser to training.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapt is the past tense of leap, meaning sprang or bounded, the same as jumped.

clue.text: Attack head, seizing power with speed

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing and holding, so the attack word clasps the power symbol inside it

parts.note: a raid is a sudden attack
P is the physics symbol for power
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness

explanation.surface: A battle plan: strike the enemy leader and grab control quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a leader to attack, but it is a headland, NESS. The attack grabs the power, not the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapidness is the noun from rapid, the quality of being fast, so it is a synonym of speed.

clue.text: Go round in circles in a hotel, struggling with cases

indicators.note: something struggling is thrashing about and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A lost guest wanders the hotel corridors, wrestling with heavy suitcases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a hotel' looks like scene-setting, but all three words are fodder along with 'cases'.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase one's tail is an idiom for busy activity that achieves nothing, like a dog circling after its own tail.

clue.text: Settled account and left

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account
quitted is an old past tense of quit, meaning left

explanation.surface: Someone paid the bill and walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled account' reads as one phrase about paying; the definition is 'Settled' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquit a debt is an old sense meaning to pay it off, so acquitted means settled.

clue.text: Tough line adopted by hospital department

parts.note: a string is a line or cord
ENT is ear, nose and throat, a hospital department

explanation.surface: A hospital ward takes a hard-line stance.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are strict and severe, which is the tough sense of the word.

clue.text: Preservative Rose spilled in shelter

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the other word

parts.note: a cote is a shelter for birds or animals, as in dovecote

indicators.note: something spilled is scattered about, so the letters lose their order

explanation.surface: Rose knocks over a tin of wood treatment in the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name or a flower; it is just four letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Creosote is an oily tar product painted onto fences and sheds to keep wood from rotting.

clue.text: Mercy shown by excellent chess player — petty officer, perhaps

parts.note: to give quarter is to show mercy to a defeated enemy
master is a title for a strong chess player

explanation.surface: A chess champion is gracious to a beaten opponent from the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mercy' sounds like a quality, but here it is the noun quarter, as in 'no quarter given'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the navy a quartermaster is a petty officer in charge of steering and signals, so 'perhaps' marks an example.

clue.text: Player, one wearing odd boots

indicators.note: a piece wearing something has it on the outside, so it sits within
odd means strange or irregular, so the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A footballer turns out in a mismatched pair of boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' and 'boots' suggest sport, but the player is a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboist plays the oboe, so is a player in the musical sense.

clue.text: Fetch feathers from shoot

parts.note: down is the soft fine feathers of a bird

explanation.surface: A gun dog retrieves feathers after a game-bird shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' looks like a noun, a shooting party, but it is the verb: to shoot a bird is to bring it down.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring down an aircraft or bird is to shoot it out of the sky, so the phrasal verb matches.

clue.text: One from Muscat? Old chap, upright character

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
the letter I is a single upright stroke

explanation.surface: A man from Muscat is described as a decent old fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright character' suggests an honest person but means the letter that stands straight up.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscat is the capital of Oman, so someone from there is an Omani; the question mark marks an example.

clue.text: I had brought back nothing from US state

indicators.note: something brought back returns the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

explanation.surface: A traveller says they came home empty-handed from an American state.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is a state in the north-western United States, so it is a direct example.

clue.text: Offensive article defending fabrication

indicators.note: defending something means standing around it to guard it, so one piece encloses the other

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece offensively stands up for a made-up story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' looks like it describes the article; it is the definition, in its sense of repugnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Alien can mean repugnant or contrary to one's nature, as in 'cruelty is alien to her', hence objectionable.

clue.text: Involved in endless attempts to catch domestic pet

indicators.note: catching something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within another
without an end means the last letter of the word for attempts is dropped

parts.note: a cat is a household pet

explanation.surface: Someone keeps trying, without success, to catch the family pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word joining 'Involved' to the wordplay, but it supplies the opening two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something involved has many interconnected parts, which is exactly what intricate means: complicated.

clue.text: Friend in Miami, golfing

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following run of words, spanning their boundary

parts.note: end of Miami plus start of golfing

explanation.surface: A pal is out on the links in Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly for Miami, with its many Spanish speakers, the answer is the Spanish word for a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for a companion and is used informally in English for a pal.

clue.text: Fuss excessively about daughter

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent frets far too much over their daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or flap, an informal noun for a fuss.

clue.text: An intuitive faculty suggesting she isn't sex mad?

indicators.note: mad means crazy or wild, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A woman's intuition is taken as proof that she is not obsessed with sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex mad' reads as a phrase about obsession, but 'mad' alone is the instruction and 'sex' is fodder with 'she isn't'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sixth sense is a supposed extra power of perception beyond the five senses, an intuition.
